prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, reaching a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18 and opening the way to precision tests of fundamental physics

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks first after reading all eight ballots. The magic-wavelength idea is simple and original: trap many neutral atoms so that the lattice light shifts the two clock levels equally, and the atoms are held without perturbing the transition. Katori proposed it and demonstrated the first strontium lattice clock. Ye then drove the systematic floor down to 10^-18 and showed what the platform can do. This is a result where every physical effect (blackbody shift, lattice light shift, collisions, relativistic redshift) has to be understood and controlled, and the agreement between independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) is exactly the reproducibility I look for. It is also the broadest-supported candidate in the room: all eight members ranked it, five placed it in their top three, and all eight proposed the same pair of names. That is not merit in itself, but the substantive arguments from Kroll, Johansson and Pearce on systematics and independent confirmation match my own reading. The physics payoff is fundamental rather than technological: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, tests of the constancy of constants and searches for new physics, with the redefinition of the second as a consequence and not as the motivation.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this is a refinement of a lineage that the committee has already honoured (Hall and Hansch with the comb in 2005, Wineland with ion clocks in 2012), so one can argue that the underlying principle, quantum-controlled precision spectroscopy, is not new. I think the magic-wavelength lattice with many atoms interrogated in parallel is a genuine conceptual step beyond single-ion clocks, but the committee should not wave the objection away. A second worry is the credit boundary: Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Hinkley, Takamoto and others did essential work, and Ye's group also contributed to the comb work already rewarded, so a two-name prize inevitably leaves out real contributors. Finally, the SI redefinition of the second has not happened, so the most visible practical consequence is still pending.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first as a measurement instrument in the strict sense, noting 10^-18 uncertainty, relativistic geodesy and dark-matter searches, and that it builds on already honoured comb and ion-clock work.
responses.response: I agree with the core assessment and share the placement. Where I would add a qualification is on applications. Geodesy and dark-matter searches are real, but I would put the citation on the 10^-18 controlled quantum system and the fundamental tests, not on the applications, because that is the argument that survives the objection that clocks are merely a refinement. I also take your point that B002 is close to your field, and I would not oppose it, but I find the label too broad and the field still developing, which is why I rank it below the clocks.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks geometric phases (Aharonov-Bohm and Berry) first as a clean, universal mechanism whose consequences are everywhere well understood, and ranks the lattice clocks only sixth.
responses.response: I ranked B008 third, so I share your admiration for the idea: it is the kind of unexpected insight about gauge potentials that I find compelling. My serious qualification is about configuration, not merit. Aharonov-Bohm is a joint 1959 discovery with David Bohm, who is deceased, so Aharonov carries the prize alone for that half, and Berry's 1984 phase has genuine precursors in Pancharatnam and in Simon's holonomy interpretation. This leaves us with two different results joined into one citation, and the argument for urgency is weaker than for the clocks, where the experimental claim is currently tested in many laboratories at a level where a wrong claim would be exposed. I would keep B008 as a serious alternative and not dismiss it, but I do not think it should be first.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first for building an instrument that was widely doubted and opening a new observational window, while placing the lattice clocks third and respecting the careful control of systematics.
responses.response: I defer to you and to Danielsson on astrophysics and on how a discovery of this scale should be weighed, and I accept that the diffuse flux is secure. My hesitation is attribution and interpretation: this is a large collaboration where the committee has to choose instigators over many analysts, and Danielsson's own ballot says the origin of most of the diffuse flux is still unexplained. The lattice clock has a compact, two-name attribution and a fully understood systematic budget. I would not block B009, but I would want the committee to say clearly which two names carry the intellectual priority before I support it.

responses.point: Olsson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, arguing that the correlated and superconducting states were widely reproduced and created a large field, and that the credited trio is a clean theory plus experiment configuration.
responses.response: This lies outside my core field, so I rely on you and the other condensed-matter members. What troubles me is timing and the mechanism: the experiments are about eight years old, the origin of the superconductivity is still unsettled, and sample dependence was a concern in the early years. I take your point that the basic phenomenology has been reproduced across graphene and TMD moire systems, and that is a real strength compared with many young fields. I would like to hear from you and Eriksson whether you see B013 as premature relative to the topological insulators, B019, which Eriksson and Mehlig both describe as mature and arguably overdue.

uncertainties: Whether the committee sees the lattice clock as a new principle or as a refinement of work honoured in 2005 and 2012.
Whether two names are enough given Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Hinkley, Takamoto and others, and how to treat Ye's earlier comb work; I am working from memory, not verified records.
How much weight to give the pending redefinition of the second, which would strengthen the case but has not happened.

Whether B034 (Cirac and Zoller) is better considered as a theory prize now, given that experimental recipients were honoured in 2012, and whether its allocation between the gate proposal and the simulation proposals is settled.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B061, B034 or B008. My long-time collaboration with Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and with the Lund and ETH attosecond groups does not concern these candidates, and nothing in the profile links me to Katori, Ye, Cirac, Zoller, Aharonov or Berry. I would flag it if attosecond or photoionization-time-delay work reached the shortlist.
